# Generalized Cosine Transforms and λ-Intersection Bodies

Intersection bodies constitute a notable class of geometric objects that occupy a central position at the crossroads of convex geometry, integral geometry, and harmonic analysis. Their significance stems from a deep connection to the study of sections of star bodies, a relationship mediated by several powerful analytical tools. In particular, Radon transforms, generalized cosine transforms, and Fourier analysis provide the machinery through which the geometric properties of these bodies can be encoded, manipulated, and ultimately understood. This interplay between geometry and analysis has proven remarkably fruitful, offering insights into longstanding problems concerning volumes and cross-sections of high-dimensional bodies.

The central focus of this article is the intricate interrelation between different kinds of generalized cosine transforms and their application to the study of a broad family of geometric objects known as λ-intersection bodies. By systematically examining how these transforms relate to one another, we develop a framework that clarifies the structure of this family and reveals the analytical principles underlying their geometric behavior.

The class of λ-intersection bodies is notable for its generality, as it encompasses several important classes of bodies that have been studied independently in the literature. Most prominently, it includes the k-intersection bodies in the sense of A. Koldobsky, which arise naturally in the investigation of sections and the resolution of problems related to the Busemann–Petty problem and its higher-dimensional analogues. Furthermore, the class contains the unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of L_p-spaces, thereby linking the geometric theory to fundamental questions in functional analysis and the isometric embedding of normed spaces.

A key contribution of this work is the demonstration that the restrictions of spherical Radon transforms and generalized cosine transforms onto lower-dimensional subspaces preserve their essential integral-geometric structure. In other words, when these operators are considered on subspaces of reduced dimension, they retain the same functional form and analytic properties that characterize them in the full-dimensional setting. This stability under restriction is a subtle but powerful phenomenon, as it allows one to transfer information between different dimensions without loss of structural coherence.

This structural result finds direct application in the investigation of sections of λ-intersection bodies. By exploiting the preservation of integral-geometric structure under restriction, the authors are able to analyze how these bodies behave when intersected with lower-dimensional subspaces. The consequences of this analysis are threefold: it yields new characterizations of the class of λ-intersection bodies, it produces illuminating examples that illustrate the scope and boundaries of the theory, and it provides new and often more transparent proofs of previously known results. In this way, the article both extends the existing body of knowledge and reorganizes it within a unified analytical perspective.

# Intersection Bodies and Generalized Cosine Transforms

## Introduction

Intersection bodies occupy a central position in modern convex geometry and geometric tomography, serving as fundamental objects that connect the study of star bodies to their lower-dimensional sections. These geometric objects derive their significance from a rich web of analytical tools—including Radon transforms, generalized cosine transforms, and Fourier analysis—that provide both the language and the methods for their investigation. The interplay between these transforms reveals deep structural properties that govern how convex and star-shaped bodies behave under sectioning by hyperplanes and lower-dimensional subspaces.

The present investigation focuses on a broad and unifying class known as λ-intersection bodies. This family is particularly noteworthy for its inclusiveness: it encompasses the well-studied k-intersection bodies as well as the unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of L_p-spaces. By working at this level of generality, one can capture a wide array of geometrically meaningful objects within a single analytical framework, thereby illuminating connections that might otherwise remain hidden when each subclass is examined in isolation.

## The Analytical Framework

At the heart of this study lies the interrelation between different generalized cosine transforms and their action on λ-intersection bodies. Generalized cosine transforms and spherical Radon transforms are integral operators defined on functions over the sphere, and they encode geometric information about how a body intersects with subspaces of a given dimension. The definition of a λ-intersection body is fundamentally analytic in nature: it involves the requirement that certain transform relationships hold between the radial function of the body and an associated measure or function. This analytic characterization is what makes the machinery of harmonic analysis and Fourier transforms so effective in this context.

The generalized cosine transforms serve as the primary vehicles for translating geometric questions about sections into analytic questions about the behavior of functions and their transforms. By understanding how one cosine transform relates to another—how they compose, invert, and constrain one another—one gains precise control over the class of bodies that can arise as λ-intersection bodies.

## Principal Results

The central contribution of this work is the demonstration that the essential integral-geometric structure of these transforms is preserved under restriction. Specifically, when spherical Radon transforms and generalized cosine transforms are restricted onto lower-dimensional subspaces, they retain their fundamental integral-geometric character. This preservation property is significant because it means that the analytical framework developed for the full-dimensional setting descends coherently to lower-dimensional situations. In practical terms, the restriction of a transform to a subspace behaves like a transform of the same type on that subspace, allowing techniques and results to be transferred across dimensions.

This structural stability has concrete consequences. It yields new characterizations of λ-intersection bodies, providing criteria by which a given star body can be recognized as belonging to this class. Furthermore, the analysis produces new examples of λ-intersection bodies, enriching the catalogue of known objects and testing the boundaries of the theory. These characterizations and examples are not merely of abstract interest; they directly advance our understanding of the sections of these bodies, which is the geometric phenomenon that motivated the entire investigation.

## Significance

By clarifying the relationships among generalized cosine transforms and establishing the invariance of their integral-geometric structure under restriction, this study strengthens the analytical foundations of the theory of intersection bodies. The results tie together the Fourier-analytic, Radon-transform, and integral-geometric perspectives, reinforcing the view that these seemingly distinct approaches are facets of a single underlying theory. In doing so, the work deepens the understanding of how star bodies relate to their sections and provides tools that are applicable across the broad landscape encompassed by the λ-intersection body framework, including the important special cases of k-intersection bodies and unit balls of subspaces of L_p.

# The Interplay of Intersection, Radon Transform, and Fourier Analysis

## Introduction

The mathematical concepts of intersection, the Radon transform, and Fourier analysis are deeply interconnected, forming a powerful framework that underpins much of modern computational imaging, signal processing, and harmonic analysis. Understanding how these ideas relate to one another reveals elegant mathematical structures with profound practical applications, particularly in fields like medical imaging and tomography.

## The Radon Transform

The Radon transform, introduced by Austrian mathematician Johann Radon in 1917, is an integral transform that takes a function defined on a plane and maps it to the set of its integrals over lines. In essence, for each line in the plane, the transform computes the integral of the function along that line.

Mathematically, given a function *f(x, y)*, the Radon transform produces projections that capture how the function accumulates along various directions and positions. This concept generalizes naturally to higher dimensions, where integration occurs over hyperplanes rather than lines.

## The Role of Intersection

Intersection plays a fundamental geometric role in understanding the Radon transform. When we consider a line passing through a two-dimensional object, the line **intersects** the object along a specific path. The Radon transform essentially measures information along these intersections.

In tomographic reconstruction, multiple lines intersect the object from different angles. The points where these lines cross—their intersections—contain overlapping information that allows us to reconstruct the original function. The geometry of these intersecting lines determines how well we can recover the internal structure of an object from its projections.

## The Fourier Connection

The relationship between the Radon transform and Fourier analysis is captured by one of the most beautiful results in the field: the **Fourier Slice Theorem** (also called the Central Slice Theorem).

This theorem states that the one-dimensional Fourier transform of a Radon projection (taken at a particular angle) equals a slice through the two-dimensional Fourier transform of the original function, taken along the same angle. In other words:

> The Fourier transform of a projection is a slice of the Fourier transform of the object.

This remarkable connection means that by collecting projections at many angles, we effectively sample the Fourier transform of our object along various lines that **intersect** at the origin of frequency space. Once enough of these frequency slices are gathered, the complete two-dimensional Fourier transform can be assembled, and the original function recovered through an inverse Fourier transform.

## Applications

The synergy between these three concepts has revolutionized several fields:

- **Medical Imaging**: Computed Tomography (CT) scanners use the Radon transform principle to reconstruct cross-sectional images of the human body from X-ray projections taken at multiple angles.

- **Signal Processing**: Fourier-based reconstruction algorithms efficiently process the intersecting projection data.

- **Astronomy and Geophysics**: These techniques help image objects that cannot be directly observed, from stellar structures to the Earth's interior.

## Conclusion

The interplay between intersection, the Radon transform, and Fourier analysis demonstrates the profound unity of mathematics. Geometric intersections provide the physical foundation, the Radon transform captures projection data, and Fourier analysis offers the computational machinery for reconstruction. Together, they form an elegant theoretical framework that continues to enable transformative technologies across science and medicine.

# Abstract

## Generalized Cosine Transforms and Sections of a Family of Intersection Bodies

We investigate a family of generalized cosine transforms acting on functions defined on the unit sphere $S^{n-1}$, and establish their fundamental interrelations through the framework of spherical harmonic decompositions and analytic continuation. For a parameter $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$, we consider the operator

$$
(\mathcal{C}^\lambda f)(\theta) = \int_{S^{n-1}} |\langle \theta, \xi \rangle|^\lambda f(\xi)\, d\xi,
$$

which unifies the classical cosine transform ($\lambda = 1$), the spherical Radon transform (arising as a limiting case), and their higher-order generalizations. We derive explicit multiplier relations expressing $\mathcal{C}^\lambda$ in terms of the Fourier–Laplace expansion, and we characterize the polynomial and singular behavior of the associated Gamma-factor multipliers at the exceptional values $\lambda = -1, 1, 3, \ldots$, where the operators degenerate or acquire distributional interpretations.

A central objective is to clarify the semigroup and intertwining properties connecting cosine transforms of differing orders. We prove that the family $\{\mathcal{C}^\lambda\}$ satisfies composition identities that permit the reduction of higher-order transforms to compositions of the first-order cosine transform with fractional powers of the Beltrami–Laplace operator. These relations furnish inversion formulas valid on suitable function spaces, including continuous, smooth, and $L^p$ settings.

As the principal geometric application, we study central sections of a one-parameter family of convex and star-shaped intersection bodies. Recall that the intersection body $IK$ of a star body $K$ is characterized through the spherical Radon transform of the radial function of $K$; the higher-order generalized cosine transforms correspond naturally to $k$-intersection bodies and their sectional volumes. We show that the $(n-1)$-dimensional volumes of hyperplane sections through the origin are governed by $\mathcal{C}^\lambda$ evaluated at the radial function raised to appropriate powers, thereby reducing questions about the geometry of sections to the analytic properties of the transform. Using the interrelations established above, we obtain:

1. **Comparison results** determining when uniformly smaller sections of one body imply volumetric inequalities, extending the Busemann–Petty phenomenon to the parametrized family.

2. **Positivity criteria** characterizing which members of the family are genuine intersection bodies, expressed via the sign of the multiplier sequence of the inverse cosine transform.

3. **Stability estimates** quantifying how perturbations of the radial function propagate to sectional volumes, with constants explicit in the harmonic multipliers.

The methods emphasize the interplay between harmonic analysis on $S^{n-1}$, the analytic continuation of Riesz-type distributions, and the convex-geometric theory of intersection bodies, suggesting further applications to Lutwak's dual Brunn–Minkowski theory and to the isomorphic geometry of sections in high dimensions.

---

*Keywords:* generalized cosine transform, spherical Radon transform, intersection bodies, Busemann–Petty problem, spherical harmonics, dual Brunn–Minkowski theory.

We investigate the interplay between the spherical Radon transform, Fourier analysis, and the geometry of star bodies, with particular emphasis on structural characterizations of intersection bodies. Building on the observation that the parallel section function of a star body admits a natural representation through the spherical Radon transform, we develop a unified analytic framework in which the class of intersection bodies arises as the image of positive distributions under this transform. Central to our approach is the Fourier-analytic characterization of intersection bodies, which identifies a convex (or star) body as an intersection body precisely when a suitable power of its radial function has a positive definite distributional Fourier transform.

Employing the theory of distributions homogeneous of degree $-1$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, we establish embedding and connection theorems relating intersection bodies to the broader classes of $k$-intersection bodies and $L_p$-star bodies. We prove that the Radon transform, viewed as an operator on even functions on the sphere $S^{n-1}$, is intimately tied to the cosine and spherical Rieszertype transforms, allowing us to translate positivity conditions between the spatial and frequency domains. As applications, we derive several new characterizations of intersection bodies in terms of curvature functionals and support functions, resolve borderline cases concerning the local behavior of radial functions, and clarify the role of intersection bodies in the solution of the Busemann–Petty problem.

Our results extend classical theorems of Busemann, Lutwak, and Koldobsky to the setting of general star bodies, and provide sharp integrability conditions under which membership in the class of intersection bodies is preserved under limits, sections, and linear transformations. We conclude by discussing open problems concerning the relationship between positive definiteness, the range of the spherical Radon transform, and the geometry of convex bodies in high dimensions.

**Keywords:** spherical Radon transform, Fourier transform of distributions, star bodies, intersection bodies, positive definite functions, Busemann–Petty problem, integral geometry.
